* **Prioritization.** The sender decides which stream's packet goes next, so new groups and audio starve old video rather than the other way around.
MoQ delivers WebRTC-like latency without the constraints of WebRTC.
Includes text chat as both an example and a core feature.

Encode and send only when someone is watching.

Every viewer lands on the nearest edge, with no regions to pick.
Dynamic announcements, connecting arbitrary publishers to subscribers.

SageOx moved from a batch flow (upload audio after the meeting, then AWS Transcribe) to MoQ. Browser, desktop, mobile and device clients publish Opus to one relay, which fans out to independent subscribers: an S3 archiver, Zoom Scribe Live transcription, and voice ID. They say adding a new consumer no longer requires another recorder or a migration.

Race-condition workaround: the archiver used to attach 70–240 ms after the browser started talking, so the first group of audio was lost. Their fix was to have the archiver subscribe to a broadcast that doesn't exist yet. The relay holds that subscription open, and only then is the client given a publish credential.

Caveat from production: a transport reported 'connected' for 42 seconds after it had stopped delivering anything. They built a separate durability receipt on a control plane, and clients release buffered audio only after the archiver confirms it is durable.

Limitation: the relay by design does not preserve packet identity or timing. To line up transcripts with speaker labels, the endpoints carry client sequence ranges on every stream, and the archived media embeds a sample-to-sequence map.

Their integration was built on outdated MoQ concepts: ANNOUNCE had been replaced by PUBLISH_NAMESPACE about 18 months earlier, there are now direct PUBLISH flows, and RENDEZVOUS_TIMEOUT covers waiting for a publisher. The author describes it as catching up on 2700 PRs.
Contributing to the moq-dev/moq repo: the author found the Rust code didn't close data streams before PUBLISH_DONE as draft-21 requires. His fix PR was merged by Luke Curley.

The author wanted one Rust MoQ implementation everywhere, including the browser, to avoid keeping a TypeScript copy in sync. Transpiling Rust to TypeScript with Charon worked, but Rust→Wasm ran at 27.9 µs per frame versus 104 µs for the best Charon build. Maintainer said Wasm is probably fine as a first step.
Commenter on the WebTransport/WebCodecs approach: Safari is still a major holdout on WebTransport with no clear update, while all other browsers have supported it in GA for 3+ years.
Commenter: an extra benefit of WebTransport over WebRTC DataChannels is that the WebTransport API works in Web Workers, so data can be sent and received off the main thread for better performance.
Commenter pushes back that a 5-second buffer isn't needed today. Using OvenMediaEngine with LL-HLS, they reached under 500 ms end-to-end from camera to browser at 20 Mbit/s with SRT or RTMP ingest.

Commenter on replacing HLS/DASH with MoQ: isn't client-side adaptive bitrate the point of HLS and DASH? With mature encoders, origins and players already out there, wouldn't it make more sense to deploy HTTP/3 within the established standards?
Skeptic: 'Replacing LLHLS and Webrtc will be hard since they both work quite well.'

Criticism of building on QUIC: it's infeasible to connect to people you don't know without ongoing approval from a corporate CA (re-approved roughly every 90 days). The commenter says this makes things brittle both technically and socially.

Industry practitioner: in most professional live cases they've seen, latency matters less than timeshifting, ad-switching, and per-program encryption keys, tracks and codecs. They prefer rebuffering over dropping video, and say the MoQ argument only considers simpler, latency-first use cases like Twitch.
Supportive commenter: 'Anything that deprecates HLS which is a piece of randomly specified and implemented crap is welcome.'
